name: Emeka Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I supervise the accounts payable team at a freight and logistics company, so five clerks paying the invoices from hauliers, fuel suppliers and port fees. Morning is the payment run, matching invoices to purchase orders and chasing the ones that don't match. Afternoon is supplier calls, approvals up to my limit and a report for the finance manager. I've been supervising for just under a year and I'm still slower at the approvals than I should be.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part of the job you're proudest of?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Spreadsheets, honestly. I've got a workbook I built myself that tracks every disputed invoice, colour-coded, and I trust it more than the company system. My girlfriend Ama, she's a physio, laughs that I talk about it like a pet. I don't use the AI stuff at all, I like to see the numbers with my own eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something like, fair enough, it was oversold. I wouldn't gloat, I'm not a gloater. Mostly I'd just get on with the payment run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved but not totally. Even small automation hits invoice matching first, because that's the most boring, routine part of my team's day. If the system matches seventy percent of invoices on its own, someone asks why I need five clerks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep my workbook going, and wait to see what the finance director actually does before I worry. Maybe learn the new matching screen if they bring one in, because I'd have to. I'd keep saving the way I always do, a fixed amount on payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a small stone in my shoe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your team's day is that routine matching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Matching is about half of my clerks' day, maybe more. Even a lazy AI that only matches invoices to orders would eat half of what my clerks do every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the team did shrink, how would you and Ama manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too bad. Ama's work is steady, I've got about nine months saved, and there are plenty of finance teams in the city. It's the job I'd miss, not the money.

say: I'd say **fair enough**, it was oversold, without gloating.
I'd just get on with the **payment run** as normal.
think: Even small automation hits **invoice matching** first.
If a system matched most invoices, someone would question **five clerks**.
do: Keep running my **own workbook** for disputed invoices.
**Wait and see** what the finance director does before worrying.
Keep saving a **fixed amount** every payday.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a small stone in his shoe.
S0.quote: Even a lazy AI that only matches invoices to orders would eat half of what my clerks do every morning.
fieldNote: Even in a calm world he spots that **routine matching** is half his team's day.
His pride is a **self-built spreadsheet**, which shows how he likes control.
Money is fine; he'd miss the **job itself** more than the pay.

steps.text: Keep the disputed-invoice workbook going every week
Wait for the finance director's plans before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to be careful, and that companies should give people time to move. At work I'd keep my head down. I don't post online, so I'd probably just talk about it with Ama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think accounts payable is finished in three years, at least the way we do it. Matching, checking and paying are all thinking tasks on that list. I'm the newest supervisor in finance, I don't use AI, so if they merge teams, I'm the one they don't keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe put an extra few hundred away a month and skip the new car. I'd look for a supervisor job at a smaller firm that's slower to change, the family-owned kind. And I'd probably still avoid the AI, if I'm honest, which I know isn't clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd sleep worse, I know that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still avoid AI, even knowing it could cost you. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's stubbornness, mostly. I've seen systems fail and I'd rather trust my own eyes. I know I should learn the AI tools, but I'd rather move to a slow, old-fashioned firm than become a man who checks a computer's homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would a slower firm buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not long, honestly. A few years, maybe. But that's a few years more.

say: I'd say companies should give people **time to move**.
At work I'd **keep my head down** and only talk to Ama.
think: Accounts payable as he knows it is **finished in three years**.
As the **newest supervisor** without AI skills, he expects to go.
do: Save an **extra few hundred** a month and skip the new car.
Look for a supervisor job at a **slower family firm**.
Keep **avoiding the AI**, knowing it isn't clever.
S1.quote: I know I should learn the AI tools, but I'd rather move to a slow, old-fashioned firm than become a man who checks a computer's homework.
fieldNote: He openly chooses escaping to a **slow firm** over learning the tools.
His stubbornness comes from having seen **systems fail** before.
Savings and a partner's steady income keep him from **alarm**.

steps.text: Put an extra few hundred a month into savings
Skip buying the new car this year
Apply for supervisor jobs at smaller family-owned firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to stay calm and wait for a plan from the government, because there'll have to be one. Nobody can stop it, so we'd have to work out how to live with it. I'd say that to my mates at football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm out of work within a year or so of it. Finance is thinking work, top to bottom. And even the slow family firms would buy it once it's cheaper than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away, no holidays, no car, and lean on Ama's income while I worked out the next thing. I'd look at the trucks side of my company, the fleet and depot work, because that's hands-on and robots are years behind. I'd hate starting at the bottom, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And a bit embarrassed that I didn't see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the conversation with Ama be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ama's the one I'd worry about telling. I'd tell my girlfriend Ama that she's paying the rent for a while, and I'd hate saying it more than I'd hate losing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The depot work buys about three years before robots. Is that enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is enough to learn the depot properly, I think. After that, I've no idea, and that's the honest answer.

say: I'd tell people to **stay calm** and wait for a government plan.
I'd say we have to learn to **live with it**.
think: He expects to be **out of work** within about a year.
Even **slow family firms** would buy AGI once it's cheaper.
do: Cut **holidays** and the car straight away.
Lean on **Ama's income** while working out the next step.
Move to the company's **fleet and depot** side, starting at the bottom.
feel: **Alarmed**, and embarrassed he didn't see it coming.
S2.quote: I'd tell my girlfriend Ama that she's paying the rent for a while, and I'd hate saying it more than I'd hate losing the job.
fieldNote: His pride is hurt by the thought of his **girlfriend paying** the rent.
He uses the **robot gap** to move to hands-on depot work.
He admits he has **no plan** beyond those three years.

steps.text: Cancel holidays and the planned car purchase
Let Ama cover the rent while he changes jobs
Ask for a junior role on the company's fleet side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people stop arguing and get moving. I'd tell younger colleagues not to train in finance admin. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd get three or four more years in payables, and then it's done. The difference from the fast one is that I can choose where I land, not just grab what's left. I'd be 32, which is still young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a transport management certificate in the first year, because I already know the hauliers and the money side. Then I'd ask to move to fleet planning in year two or three, managing drivers and trucks, which is hands-on for longer. I'd keep saving and not touch my nine months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but steadier. I could breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fleet planning has a thinking side too. Why does it feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning routes is the sort of thing AGI does too, so I know it's not perfect. I'd rather manage drivers and trucks than spreadsheets, because a lorry stuck at a port still needs a man on the phone who knows the driver's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably fine, really. He's ex-army, he'd say about time I got my hands dirty.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if people get moving.
I'd tell younger colleagues not to **train in finance admin**.
think: Payables gives him **three or four years** more.
This time he can **choose** where he lands, instead of grabbing what's left.
do: Start a **transport management** certificate in year one.
Move to **fleet planning** in year two or three.
Keep the **nine months** of savings untouched.
S3.quote: I'd rather manage drivers and trucks than spreadsheets, because a lorry stuck at a port still needs a man on the phone who knows the driver's name.
fieldNote: He moves towards **hands-on work** without moving towards AI.
He knows route planning is thinking work too, but trusts **human contact**.
Five years lets him **choose**, which matters more to him than speed.

steps.text: Enrol in a transport management certificate in year one
Ask to move to fleet planning in year two
Keep the nine months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, nobody really knows what happens, so don't panic. Plenty of predictions don't come true. That's my honest public line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably sit on it for a couple of years, and I know that's a risk. I'd be 37 when it arrives, so I'd need to have moved by then. But ten years makes it easy to tell myself next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep supervising payables for two or three years and watch. If it looked real, I'd do the transport certificate and move towards the fleet side. Meanwhile I'd pay more into my pension, because a decade of compound growth is something I do believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a low hum. Not losing sleep yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you finally act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Ama telling me to stop saying next year. A ten-year warning is the dangerous one for a man like me, because I'd keep telling myself I'll start next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything at home depend on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having kids maybe, around thirty. Ama wants two. I'd want to know my job is stable first, so it might push that back.

say: I'd say **nobody knows** what ten years brings, so people shouldn't panic.
I'd point out plenty of **predictions** don't come true.
think: He'd probably **sit on it** for a couple of years.
At **37** when it arrives, he needs to have moved by then.
do: Watch for **two or three years** before acting.
Pay more into his **pension** for ten years of growth.
Move towards the **fleet side** if it looks real.
feel: **Anxious**, a low hum without lost sleep.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning is the dangerous one for a man like me, because I'd keep telling myself I'll start next year.
fieldNote: He knows his **delay** is the real danger in the slow picture.
He trusts **compound growth** more than he trusts forecasts.
Plans for **children** depend on feeling his job is stable.

steps.text: Watch the finance team for two years before changing jobs
Push back plans for children until work feels stable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm the kind of person who needs time to change and that one gives me none. What would help is a proper government plan with a wage while you retrain, and companies being honest early about which teams are going. I can handle bad news, but I can't handle bad news that arrives the same week the job goes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I like being the one people come to with a problem invoice. It sounds small. But the clerks bring me their mess and I sort it, and I'd miss being that person.

headlineQuote: I can handle bad news, but I can't handle bad news that arrives the same week the job goes.
portrait: Emeka is **27** and supervises five accounts payable clerks at a freight and logistics company.
He trusts his **own spreadsheets**, never uses AI, and is still slow on approvals.
He has **nine months** saved and lives with his girlfriend Ama, a physiotherapist.
Under pressure he'd move to the **fleet and depot** side rather than learn AI tools.
He knows his biggest risk is **putting things off** when the warning is long.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which gives a slow changer like him no **time**.
whatWouldHelp: A **government plan** with a wage while people retrain.
Companies being **honest early** about which teams are going.
